```{r, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", eval = TRUE,
  fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4, dev.args = list(bg = "white")
)
```

A marine observation may describe a journey rather than a single location.
A trawl moves through several grid cells during a haul. An animal tracked
at intervals may also encounter different conditions between its recorded
positions. Assigning one temperature to the midpoint can miss this variation.

However, the line connecting two positions is an assumption. We do not know
that an animal followed the shortest route, moved at a constant speed or
changed depth steadily. Those choices should be visible in our analysis.

**What environmental conditions occur along a trajectory, and how do our
sampling and interpolation assumptions change its summary?**

In this tutorial we use `extract_to_track()` to follow a fictional trawl,
compare observed vertices with samples between them, and then explore a
track whose depth and time change. The temperatures come from the same
small, real Copernicus Marine subset used in the
[point extraction tutorial](extracting-environmental-data-at-points.html).
The trajectories are fictional teaching examples, not observed fishing or
animal movements. No downloads or credentials are needed.

Three modes answer different questions: use recorded vertices (the default),
sample an assumed route at explicit intervals, or split the route into
intervals at crossed grid boundaries. In every mode, environmental values
are selected using the existing point rules; they are never interpolated.

## Our research question

Imagine a trawl haul recorded at three locations. We want to describe the
deeper environmental conditions along its path, rather than use a single
representative point. We also want to know how much of that requested route
has a valid environmental value.

Here, `method = "bottom"` means the deepest valid model layer at each
sampled position. It does not establish the actual seabed depth or prove
that this was the depth occupied by the fishing gear.

## Getting started: preparing our data

Run the code from the repository's `vignettes/articles/` directory, as when
building this article. The example netCDF and its attribution accompany the
point article in `point-data/`. Drawing helpers in `buffer-data/` are shared with the buffer tutorial; all extractions use the public package functions.

```{r setup}
library(ocean3d)
nc_file <- file.path("point-data", "temperature-points.nc")
source(file.path("buffer-data", "figures.R"))

haul <- data.frame(
  haul = "haul_A",
  lon = c(-0.12, 0, 0.12),
  lat = c(37.96, 38.02, 38.08),
  date = as.Date("2026-09-20")
)
haul
```

Rows are in traversal order. The function never sorts a route by date.
With multiple tracks, `track_col` identifies which positions belong together.
Missing coordinates are rejected so an unknown gap cannot silently become
a connecting segment.

## Step 1: Extracting at the recorded positions

First, use only the supplied vertices. This provides the same environmental
selection as applying `extract_to_point()` to those coordinates.

```{r observed-vertices}
observed <- extract_to_track(
  data = haul, nc = nc_file, var = "thetao", track_col = "haul",
  sampling = "vertices", method = "bottom",
  output_col = "temperature", quiet = TRUE
)
observed$samples[c("track_id", "source_row", "lon", "lat", "temperature")]
```

The result contains three objects:

- `samples`: the positions queried, their support along the track, and values.
- `summary`: one row per track and output, with coverage and requested statistics.
- `settings`: sampling assumptions and candidate source files. These are not
  claims about which individual file supplied each value.

The summary never replaces the individual results. For example, we can save
`observed$samples` as a table and inspect or analyse each selected temperature,
just as we would after point extraction.

```{r inspect-individual-values}
observed$samples[c("sample_id", "lon", "lat", "temperature")]

# To save the individual results when running this tutorial manually:
# write.csv(observed$samples, "haul_sample_temperatures.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

## Step 2: Sampling the path between vertices

There are four ways to decide where environmental values are requested:

| `sampling` | Positions queried | When it is useful | Example case |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| `"vertices"` | Only the supplied observations; the default without steps. | Preserve the original sampling. | Attach conditions to recorded tag locations without assuming intermediate positions. |
| `"balanced"` | One shared subdivision satisfying distance, depth and elapsed-time limits. | Respect every maximum without adding redundant step grids. | Sample an assumed dive between tag records, limiting changes in kilometres, metres and hours together. |
| `"merged_steps"` | Combine distance/depth cuts with temporal cuts. | Retain both step grids, including close neighbours. | Check how adding time-driven queries changes the results of a depth-sampled dive. |
| `"cells"` | Midpoints of intervals defined by crossed cells and changes of layer or time. | Represent crossed grid intervals, including return visits. | Describe the environmental cells crossed by a trawl, retaining separate visits when it returns to a cell. |

Every inserted position belongs to the same assumed trajectory. These modes
change where it is queried, not which route the animal is assumed to follow.
They do not interpolate environmental values.

Balanced sampling inserts positions along the connecting route.
Here, adjacent samples are at most one horizontal kilometre apart.
This distance is a maximum: the function keeps all supplied vertices and
divides each original segment into equal parts, so some intervals are shorter.

```{r sample-route}
route <- extract_to_track(
  data = haul, nc = nc_file, var = "thetao", track_col = "haul",
  sampling = "balanced", spacing_km = 1, method = "bottom",
  statistics = c("mean", "sd", "se", "min", "max"),
  output_col = "temperature", quiet = TRUE
)
head(route$samples[c(
  "sample_id", "source_row", "is_interpolated", "distance_km", "temperature"
)])
route$summary
```

### Counting observed and assumed positions

The result records how much sampling was added for each track:

```{r sampling-counts}
route$settings$sampling_counts
route$summary[c("track_id", "n_observed", "n_assumed", "n_samples", "n_valid")]
```

`n_observed` counts supplied vertices; `n_assumed` counts inserted positions;
`n_samples` is their total. `n_valid` belongs to each environmental output and
counts values eligible for its summary. Missing results and invalid marine
connections do not erase positions from the sampling counts. In cells mode,
the assumed positions are interval midpoints, not new observations.

`settings$sampling_counts` has one row per track, however many variables are
extracted. It remains available with `statistics = NULL`. The summary repeats
these track counts for each output; they should not be added across outputs.
No extra console report is printed for every generated position.

`source_row` identifies a supplied vertex. An inserted position has
`is_interpolated = TRUE` and `source_row = NA`: it is not a new observation.
Non-coordinate vertex attributes are also `NA` between observations.
The generated `track_id` remains available for every sample.

**This interpolates the path, not the temperature.** Each inserted location
is passed to `extract_to_point()` with the usual cell, depth and time
selection rules. Several nearby samples can therefore select the same
environmental value. No interpolation between environmental grid values
has been performed.

A one-kilometre spacing can select the same grid cell several times. That is
expected: these are positions along the route, not a list of unique cells.
Conversely, a route can cross a narrow corner of a cell between samples
without ever querying it. Smaller spacing reduces this risk but cannot
guarantee that every intersected cell is represented.

One result per crossed cell would be a different sampling mode, not simply
removing duplicate temperatures. Two cells can have the same temperature;
the same cell can also be visited again at another depth or time. Those
visits may represent different environmental conditions and must not be
silently collapsed.

```{r route-map, fig.cap="Figure 1. Recorded vertices and the sampled route. Inserted positions represent an assumed path; colour shows the selected deeper temperature."}
plot_track_map(route$samples, observed$samples)
```

Positions follow shortest WGS84 geodesics. Distances are horizontal; they do
not include vertical travel. Routes near the antimeridian follow the short
connection. Antipodal endpoints need an intermediate waypoint.

Without a sampling request, only the original vertices are used. Supplying
`spacing_km` explicitly requests balanced sampling. No grid-based spacing is
silently inferred. You can also set `sampling = "balanced"` with a depth or
time step, use `sampling = "merged_steps"` to retain both sets of step cuts,
or use `sampling = "cells"` for grid intervals. All original vertices are
retained. Equal spacing is defined within each original segment; adjacent
segments may have different spacing.

### Following crossed cells, including repeat visits

```{r crossed-cells}
crossed <- extract_to_track(
  haul, nc_file, var = "thetao", track_col = "haul",
  sampling = "cells", method = "bottom", output_col = "temperature",
  quiet = TRUE
)
intervals <- subset(crossed$samples, sample_kind == "cell_interval")
head(intervals[c("segment_id", "segment_start_fraction",
                 "segment_end_fraction", "support_km", "temperature")])
crossed$summary
```

Each interval uses the midpoint of the portion inside the selected cell.
Its weight is the full interval's distance or duration. Original vertices
are also retained, labelled `observation`, with zero interval support.
They do not add extra weight to the cells-mode summary. Returning to a cell
on a later segment remains a separate visit. Changes in selected depth or
timestamp can also divide an interval. Separate original segments remain
separate even if their selected environmental record is identical.

Intersections are calculated numerically for rectilinear grids and the
existing selection rules. They do not reconstruct the physical averaging
period represented by a timestamp. Cells mode currently requires spatial
within matching and standard temporal precision; use vertices or balanced
sampling for spatial nearest matching or custom temporal precision.
Overlapping sources with different horizontal grids must first be aligned
explicitly, or used with balanced sampling; this avoids guessing where the
winning source changes between incompatible grids.

The per-output diagnostic gives the record actually selected:

```{r actual-provenance}
crossed$samples$temperature_match_info[[1]]
```

`settings$candidate_sources` lists files considered. In contrast, each
`temperature_match_info` describes the file, cell, layer and time that
actually supplied that sample. A missing output has no assigned selected
source. This avoids attributing an extracted value to the first input file.

## Step 3: Understanding the summary weights

Before choosing a mean, decide what should have equal importance: each
sampled position, each kilometre travelled, or each minute spent on the route.
The same selected temperatures can give different means because these are
different scientific questions.

### Equal weight: what is the average sampled value?

With `weighting = "equal"`, every sampled position receives the same weight.
This is the ordinary arithmetic mean. It can be useful when each supplied
observation should count equally. With irregular sampling, a densely recorded
part of a track has more influence even if it represents little distance or time.

### Distance weight: what conditions describe the travelled route?

With `weighting = "distance"`, a sample represents half the distance to the
previous sample plus half the distance to the next. An endpoint receives
only its adjacent half-segment. These lengths add to the entire requested
track length.

For example, if three consecutive samples are at 0, 1 and 4 km, their
distance supports are 0.5, 2 and 1.5 km. The middle sample receives half the
first kilometre plus half the next three kilometres. The weights sum to 4 km,
not three samples.

```{r sample-support}
head(route$samples[c("sample_id", "distance_km", "support_km")])
sum(route$samples$support_km)
route$summary$total_distance_km
```

The mean uses those lengths as weights. This is a numerical approximation
to conditions along the route. It differs from the area, depth thickness
and duration weights used by `extract_to_buffer()`.

### Duration weight: what conditions describe time spent along the route?

With `weighting = "duration"`, the same half-interval rule uses elapsed time.
If our three samples were recorded at 10:00, 11:30 and 12:00, their supports
would be 45, 60 and 15 minutes. The track spends 90 minutes in its first
kilometre and only 30 minutes in its next three kilometres. A mean describing
time spent should therefore differ from a mean describing distance travelled.

Durations are measured between actual UTC instants. They are not counts of
dates or environmental timestamps. A stationary animal can have positive time
support even when its horizontal distance support is zero.

### The same three temperatures, three different answers

The following small numerical example illustrates the weights independently
of our Copernicus data. The temperatures are invented teaching values.

```{r illustrative-weights}
weight_example <- data.frame(
  sample = c("A", "B", "C"),
  temperature = c(10, 20, 30),
  distance_support_km = c(0.5, 2, 1.5),
  duration_support_minutes = c(45, 60, 15)
)
knitr::kable(weight_example)

weight_comparison <- data.frame(
  question = c("Average sample", "Average kilometre", "Average minute"),
  weighting = c("equal", "distance", "duration"),
  mean_temperature = c(
    mean(weight_example$temperature),
    weighted.mean(weight_example$temperature, weight_example$distance_support_km),
    weighted.mean(weight_example$temperature, weight_example$duration_support_minutes)
  )
)
knitr::kable(weight_comparison, digits = 2)
```

Equal weighting gives **20 degrees C**, distance weighting **22.5 degrees C**,
and duration weighting **17.5 degrees C**. No temperature was changed: only
what each temperature represents in the mean.

```{r weighting-figure, fig.cap="Figure 2. The three sampled temperatures receive different shares of the total weight. A, B and C are the same samples in all three comparisons."}
weight_shares <- cbind(
  Equal = rep(1 / 3, 3),
  Distance = weight_example$distance_support_km /
    sum(weight_example$distance_support_km),
  Duration = weight_example$duration_support_minutes /
    sum(weight_example$duration_support_minutes)
)
barplot(
  weight_shares, beside = TRUE, col = grDevices::hcl.colors(3, "Viridis"),
  ylim = c(0, 0.75), ylab = "Share of total weight",
  legend.text = c("A: 10 C", "B: 20 C", "C: 30 C"),
  args.legend = list(x = "top", horiz = TRUE, bty = "n", cex = 0.85)
)
```

### Applying each choice to our real-data example

We already have the distance-weighted result. First compare it with equal
weighting, keeping the same positions and environmental selections.

```{r compare-weights}
equal <- extract_to_track(
  data = haul, nc = nc_file, var = "thetao", track_col = "haul",
  spacing_km = 1, method = "bottom", weighting = "equal",
  output_col = "temperature", quiet = TRUE
)
data.frame(
  distance_weighted = route$summary$mean,
  equal_sample_weight = equal$summary$mean
)
```

Equal weighting gives every sampled position the same importance. It can
overrepresent parts of a track with denser sampling. Distance weighting
reduces that dependence, but a coarse route can still miss environmental
changes between samples.

To illustrate duration weighting, add fictional UTC times to the same three
recorded positions. The first segment now takes 90 minutes and the second
30 minutes. We explicitly allow interpolation of time between these records.

```{r real-duration-weights}
timed_haul <- haul
timed_haul$date <- as.POSIXct(c(
  "2026-09-20 10:00:00", "2026-09-20 11:30:00", "2026-09-20 12:00:00"
), tz = "UTC")

duration <- extract_to_track(
  timed_haul, nc_file, var = "thetao", track_col = "haul",
  spacing_km = 1, method = "bottom", interpolate_time = TRUE,
  time_resolution = "daily", weighting = "duration",
  output_col = "temperature", quiet = TRUE
)
data.frame(
  weighting = c("distance", "equal", "duration"),
  mean_temperature = c(
    route$summary$mean, equal$summary$mean, duration$summary$mean
  )
)
sum(duration$samples$support_seconds) / 60
```

The total duration is 120 minutes. All these times select the same UTC day,
so the comparison changes the weights rather than choosing different daily
environmental records. Differences can be small if the field changes little
along this particular route; the invented example above makes their meaning
easier to see.

Missing environmental samples remain in the total requested distance, time
or sample count when calculating `valid_fraction`. They are not silently
removed from the coverage denominator. The mean uses valid values only
after the requested coverage threshold has been met.

SD, SE, minimum and maximum use the same definitions as in the buffer
function. **SE assumes independent samples.** Densifying a trajectory
does not create independent observations, so SE should not be interpreted
as an automatic measure of environmental uncertainty. The reported
`effective_n` describes the weights, not the number of independent cells.

`variation_status` explains the SD/SE columns separately from overall coverage:

| Value | Meaning |
|:--|:--|
| `not_requested` | Neither SD nor SE was requested; this is normal for mean-only summaries. |
| `available` | The requested SD/SE values are finite and available. |
| `insufficient_samples` | Coverage was accepted, but fewer than two valid samples remain for SD/SE. |
| `not_available` | Coverage/support was rejected, or SD/SE is not finite. Check `status` and the requested statistics. |

For example, `statistics = "mean"` gives `not_requested`, while requesting
`statistics = c("mean", "sd", "se")` can give `available`. A complete track
does not imply independent samples or guarantee a finite SD/SE for extreme data.

## Step 4: Checking whether the spacing is fine enough

Try several spacings and compare the summaries. Convergence helps assess
the approximation for this particular track and field; it cannot prove
that every crossed cell was visited.

```{r compare-spacings}
half_km <- extract_to_track(
  haul, nc_file, var = "thetao", track_col = "haul",
  spacing_km = 0.5, method = "bottom", output_col = "temperature", quiet = TRUE
)
two_km <- extract_to_track(
  haul, nc_file, var = "thetao", track_col = "haul",
  spacing_km = 2, method = "bottom", output_col = "temperature", quiet = TRUE
)
data.frame(
  maximum_spacing_km = c(2, 1, 0.5),
  samples = c(nrow(two_km$samples), nrow(route$samples), nrow(half_km$samples)),
  mean = c(two_km$summary$mean, route$summary$mean, half_km$summary$mean)
)
```

## Step 5: Choosing whether to interpolate depth and time

Now imagine two animal locations with different depths and timestamps.
Neither a straight depth change nor constant speed is guaranteed between
them. The function therefore requires an explicit choice.

```{r changing-track}
dive <- data.frame(
  lon = c(-0.10, 0.10), lat = c(37.98, 38.06),
  depth = c(30, 180),
  date = as.POSIXct(c("2026-09-20 00:00:00", "2026-09-21 00:00:00"), tz = "UTC")
)
```

Without permission to interpolate changing required coordinates, balanced
sampling fails with an explanation rather than silently inventing depths
or times.

```{r interpolation-needed, error=TRUE}
extract_to_track(dive, nc_file, var = "thetao", spacing_km = 2, quiet = TRUE)
```

We can explicitly assume that depth and elapsed UTC time change linearly
along each segment. Optional step limits add samples when a segment changes
rapidly in depth or time, even if it moves little horizontally.

For a segment from 20 m at 10:00 to 100 m at 11:00, its halfway position is
assigned 60 m and 10:30. This assumes uniform progress along that segment;
it does not establish where the animal really was between observations.

Horizontal distance, depth and time limits are checked together. For example,
a two-kilometre horizontal limit, a ten-metre depth limit and a one-hour time
limit mean that enough samples are inserted to satisfy all three.
With `balanced`, elapsed-time limits produce one common subdivision:

1. The route is about 19.7 km long, requiring at least 10 intervals at 2 km.
2. Depth changes by 150 m, requiring at least 15 intervals at 10 m.
3. Time advances by 24 hours, requiring at least 24 intervals at one hour.
4. The largest requirement is 24, so the function makes 24 equal intervals:
   about 0.82 km, 6.25 m and one hour each, with 25 positions including endpoints.

These are maximum changes, not three exact spacings that must occur together.
No separate set of ten-metre positions is added to the hourly positions.
A stationary track can still need extra samples because depth or time changes.

```{r assumed-dive}
# Record and display any scientific warnings from the inherited point selection.
dive_result <- extract_to_track(
  dive, nc_file, var = "thetao", sampling = "balanced", spacing_km = 2,
  interpolate_depth = TRUE, interpolate_time = TRUE,
  depth_step_m = 10, time_step = 1, time_unit = "hours",
  time_resolution = "daily", method = "nearest",
  output_col = "temperature", quiet = TRUE
)
head(dive_result$samples[c("lon", "lat", "depth", "date", "temperature")])
dive_result$settings$sampling_counts
```

`time_step = 1, time_unit = "hours"` specifies a maximum one-hour step. This controls sampling of the assumed trajectory; it does not
change the environmental dataset's temporal resolution. Linear interpolation
is performed only when requested, and missing endpoint depths or times do
not become invented intermediate measurements.

### Keeping separate step cuts with `merged_steps`

Sometimes we want to query both sets of step positions. `merged_steps` keeps
the distance/depth subdivision and adds the temporal subdivision, removing
coincident positions. For this dive, the first set has 15 intervals (10 m each)
and the second has 24 (one hour each). Their union has 37 positions.

```{r merged-dive}
merged_dive <- extract_to_track(
  dive, nc_file, var = "thetao", sampling = "merged_steps", spacing_km = 2,
  interpolate_depth = TRUE, interpolate_time = TRUE,
  depth_step_m = 10, time_step = 1, time_unit = "hours",
  time_resolution = "daily", method = "nearest",
  output_col = "temperature", quiet = TRUE
)
merged_dive$settings$sampling_counts
```

For example, it queries 11:00 at 98.75 m, 11:12 at 100 m and 12:00 at 105 m.
Balanced sampling queries 11:00 and 12:00 here, already satisfying every limit.
Both modes assume the same trajectory; the additional sample does not provide
an additional observation or reveal an environmental detail absent from the grid.

```{r sampling-timelines, fig.cap="Figure 3. Each dot is a requested position on the same assumed dive. Balanced sampling uses one common hourly subdivision; merged steps also retain the ten-metre subdivision."}
balanced_hours <- as.numeric(difftime(
  dive_result$samples$date, dive$date[1], units = "hours"
))
merged_hours <- as.numeric(difftime(
  merged_dive$samples$date, dive$date[1], units = "hours"
))
old_par <- par(mar = c(4, 7, 1, 1))
plot(
  balanced_hours, rep(2, length(balanced_hours)),
  xlim = c(0, 24), ylim = c(0.5, 2.5), yaxt = "n", pch = 16,
  col = "#0072B2", xlab = "Elapsed time (hours)", ylab = ""
)
axis(2, at = c(1, 2), labels = c("Merged steps", "Balanced"), las = 1)
points(merged_hours, rep(1, length(merged_hours)), pch = 16, col = "#D55E00")
par(old_par)
```

### Calendar months and years

Seconds, minutes, hours and days are elapsed-time units; one day is 24 hours
in UTC. Months and years have variable lengths and must be whole numbers.
For these units, the function retains calendar anchors, advancing from the
preceding anchor and clamping to the destination month's last day. For example,
31 January 2020 leads to 29 February, then 29 March.

Balanced sampling divides each calendar span into equal parts only if required
by distance or depth. It does not add a second global set of spatial cuts.
For example, if a span covers 100 km with a 30 km limit, it is divided into four
25 km intervals. Different calendar spans can have different elapsed durations
and subdivisions: this exception preserves calendar meaning rather than treating
every month as a fixed number of days. `merged_steps` instead combines the global
distance/depth cuts with those calendar anchors.

Here, `daily` deliberately selects by UTC calendar labels. It does not
reconstruct hourly temperatures from a daily product. With `auto`, the
precision of the original observations controls matching, before inserting
samples. `Date` uses daily comparison; explicit date-times retain hours.

```{r assumed-dive-3d, fig.cap="Figure 4. The assumed three-dimensional trajectory, coloured by selected model temperature. Depth is the requested path depth, not an interpolated environmental layer."}
track_explorer(dive_result$samples)
```

Rotate the figure and inspect the hover labels. Requested depths vary
smoothly along the assumed route, but selected environmental values may
change in steps. They still come from the existing grid layers and records.
The three display axes are scaled separately for readability; the view is
not a physical scale model of horizontal distance versus depth.

For time spent along the route, use `weighting = "duration"`. Its support
is measured in elapsed seconds, not the number of dates. Missing endpoint
times leave unknown time support, so a duration summary becomes `NA`.
Stationary tracks can have a duration summary even though their horizontal
distance is zero.

```{r elapsed-summary}
elapsed <- extract_to_track(
  dive, nc_file, var = "thetao", spacing_km = 2,
  interpolate_depth = TRUE, interpolate_time = TRUE,
  time_resolution = "daily", weighting = "duration", quiet = TRUE
)
elapsed$summary
```

## Step 6: Recognising gaps and partial environmental coverage

The default spatial selection requires a sample to lie inside a cell.
A route extending beyond the source can therefore have valid values along
one part and `NA` along another. Those missing samples remain in the total
requested support used for the summary threshold.

```{r partial-route}
outside <- haul[c(1, 3), ]
outside$lon[2] <- 0.4
partial <- extract_to_track(
  outside, nc_file, var = "thetao", track_col = "haul",
  spacing_km = 1, method = "bottom", quiet = TRUE
)
partial$summary[c("valid_fraction", "status", "mean")]
```

By default, at least 80% of the requested support must have a valid value.
Lower the threshold only if a partial route answers your scientific question.
This fraction is based on sampled support; it is not an exact geometric
measurement of the line inside the source.

### Allowing a nearby cell when the sample is outside coverage

`spatial_match = "within"`, the default, asks for a cell containing the
requested position. If none supplies a valid value, that output is `NA`.
`spatial_match = "nearest"` instead permits selection of a nearby valid cell
under the existing point-selection rules. An explicit `max_distance_km`
limits the distance from the requested position to the selected cell centre.
If no acceptable candidate is within that limit, the output remains `NA`.

```{r nearest-route}
nearby <- extract_to_track(
  outside, nc_file, var = "thetao", track_col = "haul",
  sampling = "balanced", spacing_km = 1, method = "bottom",
  spatial_match = "nearest", max_distance_km = 30, quiet = TRUE
)
partial$summary[c("valid_fraction", "status", "mean")]
nearby$summary[c("valid_fraction", "status", "mean")]
tail(nearby$samples[c("lon", "lat", "thetao")], 3)
tail(nearby$samples$thetao_match_info, 1)
```

Here we deliberately allow a cell centre up to 30 km away. The diagnostic
shows the actual selected location and distance. The requested coordinates
stay unchanged. This does not draw a 30 km buffer, average neighbouring cells
or move the trajectory to that cell. It changes which environmental record
may represent a sample, so the limit needs a scientific justification.
Nearest spatial matching is available with vertices, balanced and merged
steps; cells mode uses within matching.

### Rejecting an implausible connection or an oversized request

These limits answer different questions:

| Argument | What it limits | What happens if exceeded |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `max_distance_km` | Sample-to-selected-cell-centre distance with nearest matching. | No acceptable candidate gives `NA`. |
| `max_segment_km` | Horizontal distance between two successive original vertices. | Stop before environmental extraction. |
| `max_gap_hours` | Elapsed time between two successive original vertices. | Stop before environmental extraction. |
| `max_samples` | Total positions requested across all tracks. | Stop instead of constructing an oversized result. |

The last three are safeguards, not instructions to interpolate more points
or fill gaps. Their limits should reflect the observation system and the
size of the intended analysis. These deliberately strict examples stop:

```{r segment-limit-example, error=TRUE}
# The dive covers about 19.7 km between its two observations.
extract_to_track(dive, nc_file, var = "thetao", max_segment_km = 5)
```

```{r time-gap-example, error=TRUE}
# Its original observations are 24 hours apart, exceeding this six-hour limit.
extract_to_track(dive, nc_file, var = "thetao", max_gap_hours = 6)
```

```{r sample-budget-example, error=TRUE}
# A one-metre spacing would require far more than 100 positions.
extract_to_track(
  haul, nc_file, var = "thetao", spacing_km = 0.001, max_samples = 100
)
```

## Step 7: Checking whether a proposed route is marine

A connecting line is not necessarily a plausible marine route. Two locations
can both be at sea while their shortest connecting segment crosses a peninsula
or island. More closely spaced environmental queries do not resolve that
problem: they still follow the same assumed line.

Marine connectivity can be checked with a supplied polygon or raster mask. A finite
temperature is not proof that the route stays at sea, and an environmental
`NA` is not proof of land. It may instead mean missing source coverage,
an unavailable timestamp, depth or environmental value.

### Two marine endpoints do not guarantee a marine connection

The following example uses a **fictional island**, not a real coastline.
It demonstrates the geometry check separately from environmental extraction.
The same two endpoints are connected directly or by deliberately supplied
illustrative waypoints. The second line is drawn to explain the distinction;
the package has not discovered or recommended a route around the island.

```{r illustrative-land}
island <- sf::st_sfc(sf::st_polygon(list(rbind(
  c(-0.025, 37.99), c(0.025, 37.99), c(0.025, 38.05),
  c(-0.025, 38.05), c(-0.025, 37.99)
))), crs = 4326)

endpoints <- data.frame(lon = c(-0.10, 0.10), lat = 38.02)
endpoints_sf <- sf::st_as_sf(endpoints, coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326)

connections <- sf::st_sf(
  connection = c("Direct connection", "Illustrative waypoints"),
  geometry = sf::st_sfc(
    sf::st_linestring(as.matrix(endpoints)),
    sf::st_linestring(rbind(
      c(-0.10, 38.02), c(-0.04, 38.075),
      c(0.04, 38.075), c(0.10, 38.02)
    )),
    crs = 4326
  )
)

# Use a projected CRS for this small, local geometry demonstration.
island_projected <- sf::st_transform(island, 3857)
connections_projected <- sf::st_transform(connections, 3857)
endpoints_projected <- sf::st_transform(endpoints_sf, 3857)

data.frame(
  endpoint = c("Start", "End"),
  intersects_land = lengths(sf::st_intersects(
    endpoints_projected, island_projected
  )) > 0
)

land_check <- data.frame(
  connection = connections$connection,
  intersects_land = lengths(sf::st_intersects(
    connections_projected, island_projected
  )) > 0
)
land_check
```

Both endpoint checks return `FALSE`: neither recorded endpoint lies on the
fictional island. The direct line nevertheless returns `TRUE`, while the
illustrative line with extra waypoints returns `FALSE`. Checking only the
endpoints, or only sparse environmental samples, would miss this distinction.

```{r land-crossing-figure, fig.cap="Figure 5. A fictional island illustrates why the whole connecting line needs checking. The red connection crosses land despite having both endpoints at sea. The blue line uses manually specified illustrative waypoints; no automatic rerouting has been performed."}
plot(
  NA, xlim = c(-0.14, 0.14), ylim = c(37.95, 38.115),
  asp = 1 / cos(38 * pi / 180),
  xlab = "Longitude (degrees east)", ylab = "Latitude (degrees north)"
)
rect(par("usr")[1], par("usr")[3], par("usr")[2], par("usr")[4],
     col = "aliceblue", border = NA)
plot(island, add = TRUE, col = "wheat", border = "tan4")
plot(sf::st_geometry(connections)[1], add = TRUE,
     col = "firebrick", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
plot(sf::st_geometry(connections)[2], add = TRUE,
     col = "steelblue4", lwd = 2)

# Highlight the portion of the direct line that intersects the island.
crossing_part <- sf::st_intersection(
  sf::st_geometry(connections_projected)[1], island_projected
)
plot(sf::st_transform(crossing_part, 4326), add = TRUE,
     col = "firebrick", lwd = 6)
points(endpoints$lon, endpoints$lat, pch = 21, bg = "white", cex = 1.3)
text(0, 38.043, "Fictional island", cex = 0.7)
legend(
  "bottom", inset = 0.02, bty = "n", cex = 0.75,
  legend = c("Direct connection", "Illustrative waypoints", "Recorded endpoints"),
  col = c("firebrick", "steelblue4", "black"),
  lty = c(2, 1, NA), lwd = c(2, 2, NA), pch = c(NA, NA, 21), pt.bg = "white"
)
```

### Applying that check during extraction

The illustration above makes the geometric question visible. Now apply
the integrated mask option to the same endpoints and environmental source.

```{r integrated-mask}
domain <- sf::st_sfc(sf::st_polygon(list(rbind(
  c(-0.2, 37.8), c(0.2, 37.8), c(0.2, 38.2),
  c(-0.2, 38.2), c(-0.2, 37.8)
))), crs = 4326)
marine_route <- transform(endpoints, date = as.Date("2026-09-20"))
checked <- extract_to_track(
  marine_route, nc_file, var = "thetao", method = "bottom",
  spacing_km = 1, land_mask = island, mask_type = "land",
  mask_domain = domain, quiet = TRUE
)
checked$samples[c("source_row", "segment_status", "thetao")]
checked$summary[c("valid_fraction", "status", "mean")]
```

The original observations remain available. Values along the invalid
connection are `NA`, and its distance remains in the coverage denominator.
The function does not join another point across that connection. Use
`land_policy = "error"` to stop instead.

### What does the polygon tell us about the sea?

The previous call uses `mask_type = "land"`: the island polygon means land.
`mask_domain = domain` declares where that land information is complete enough
to interpret the rest as sea. Outside that domain, absence of a land polygon
does not establish that the route is marine. Both geometries need a CRS.

If we omit the domain, a connection crossing the island can still be rejected
as land. A connection that misses the island has unknown mask coverage:

```{r mask-domain-example}
northern_route <- marine_route
northern_route$lat <- 38.09
unknown <- extract_to_track(
  northern_route, nc_file, var = "thetao", method = "bottom",
  spacing_km = 1, land_mask = island, mask_type = "land", quiet = TRUE
)
unknown$samples[c("source_row", "segment_status", "thetao")]
known <- extract_to_track(
  northern_route, nc_file, var = "thetao", method = "bottom",
  spacing_km = 1, land_mask = island, mask_type = "land",
  mask_domain = domain, quiet = TRUE
)
known$samples[c("source_row", "segment_status", "thetao")]
```

The first call marks the connecting segment `unknown_mask_coverage`: missing
the island does not establish known sea. With the declared complete domain,
the northern connection is classified `marine`. Original observations remain
in both results; the classification concerns their assumed connection.

Only use a domain where the mask actually supports that interpretation;
drawing a large rectangle does not improve an incomplete coastline dataset.
Our rectangle and island are fictional teaching data.

If the polygons instead delineate known sea, use `mask_type = "marine"`.
For this example, derive the marine area by removing the island from the domain:

```{r marine-polygon-example}
sea_polygon <- sf::st_transform(sf::st_difference(
  sf::st_transform(domain, 3857), sf::st_transform(island, 3857)
), 4326)
marine_mask_result <- extract_to_track(
  northern_route, nc_file, var = "thetao", method = "bottom",
  spacing_km = 1, land_mask = sea_polygon, mask_type = "marine", quiet = TRUE
)
marine_mask_result$samples[c("source_row", "segment_status", "thetao")]
```

The whole connection must lie strictly inside the known marine area.
Touching its boundary is rejected conservatively. A land polygon and a
marine polygon therefore have different meanings; choose the matching option.

### Using a raster with explicit sea and land codes

Here is a small fictional one-layer raster for the same region:

```{r raster-mask-example, fig.cap="Figure 6. The fictional raster mask uses 0 for land and 1 for known sea. Raster cells approximate the island; the red connection crosses land."}
sea_raster <- terra::rast(
  nrows = 40, ncols = 40, xmin = -0.2, xmax = 0.2,
  ymin = 37.8, ymax = 38.2, crs = "EPSG:4326"
)
terra::values(sea_raster) <- 1  # Known sea.
sea_raster <- terra::rasterize(
  terra::vect(island), sea_raster, field = 0, background = 1, touches = TRUE
)
terra::plot(sea_raster, col = c("wheat", "aliceblue"))
terra::lines(terra::vect(connections), col = c("firebrick", "steelblue4"), lwd = 2)
raster_result <- extract_to_track(
  marine_route, nc_file, var = "thetao", method = "bottom", spacing_km = 1,
  land_mask = sea_raster, marine_values = 1, quiet = TRUE
)
raster_result$samples[c("source_row", "segment_status", "thetao")]
```

The red direct connection intersects cells coded as land and is classified
`land_crossing`. The blue line illustrates the alternative waypoints from the
earlier figure; this call extracts the direct route only. The stair-step island
edge reflects raster resolution, not extra detail about a real coastline.

`marine_values = 1` states which code means sea; other finite codes mean land.
Raster `NA` cells and locations outside its extent mean unknown, not sea,
and invalidate the affected connection. `mask_domain` is for polygon masks;
the raster's extent and NA cells describe its known domain instead.
Categorical rasters use their underlying numeric codes, not printed labels.
Geographic rasters must use -180 to 180 degree longitudes: rotate or reproject
other conventions explicitly. Antimeridian connections are split before queries.

### Checking the connection, not just environmental sample points

The check follows the complete connecting polyline, independently of
environmental query spacing. `mask_step_km = 0.5` limits the segments used
to approximate the WGS84 geodesic. Both that approximation and coastline
resolution affect accuracy. Contact with land counts as intersection.
Use a mask appropriate to your study scale; a finite temperature does not
prove marine connectivity. With no mask, `segment_status` is `not_checked`.

For example, `spacing_km = 5` may request temperature only every few kilometres,
while `mask_step_km = 0.5` represents the curved geodesic with line segments
no longer than about 500 m for the mask check. Each entire segment is tested
against the mask; this is not a land check only at 500 m sample points.
Reducing this step follows geodesic curvature more closely, but cannot add
coastline detail missing from the mask. Touching the island still counts as
crossing, even if every environmental query happens to fall outside it.

An automatic shortest marine route could be a future alternative, but it
would require a routing grid, its resolution and additional scientific
assumptions. It is not implemented. Supply justified waypoints or split the
track instead of treating a computed detour as an observed route.

## Step 8: Working with LINESTRING features

A spatial line can supply its coordinates directly. Its CRS is required;
projected lines are transformed to longitude and latitude. A date or depth
may be constant for the whole feature, or supplied as a list with one value
per vertex. Each feature must have a distinct track ID.

```{r sf-line}
line <- sf::st_sf(
  haul = "haul_A", date = as.Date("2026-09-20"),
  geometry = sf::st_sfc(sf::st_linestring(as.matrix(haul[c("lon", "lat")])),
                        crs = 4326)
)
line_result <- extract_to_track(
  line, nc_file, var = "thetao", track_col = "haul", spacing_km = 1,
  method = "bottom", quiet = TRUE
)
line_result$summary
```

Multipart lines are rejected: split disconnected parts explicitly instead
of joining them. For XYZ lines, `z_as_depth = TRUE` confirms that Z is metres
positive downwards. Elevation, negative depth and M coordinates are not
silently reinterpreted.

## Summary

We have followed a recorded line through the environmental grid, inspected
inserted positions, and compared distance-weighted and equal-sample summaries.
We have also compared duration weighting, made depth and time assumptions
explicit, and checked the effect of sample spacing and incomplete environmental
coverage. We have distinguished an assumed connection from a route validated
against land information.

Use [point extraction](extracting-environmental-data-at-points.html) for
recorded locations and [buffer extraction](extracting-and-weighting-buffer-data.html)
for environmental support around an observation. Track extraction adds an
assumed connecting route. For environmental support around each position,
continue with [buffered tracks](extracting-buffers-along-tracks.html).
Environmental interpolation and automatic marine routing are not performed.

Environmental data: E.U. Copernicus Marine Service Information;
[doi:10.48670/mds-00375](https://doi.org/10.48670/mds-00375). The
[point tutorial](extracting-environmental-data-at-points.html) documents
the subset, licence and preparation. The trajectories are fictional.

## All arguments and defaults

<details open>
<summary>Expand or collapse the complete extract_to_track() signature</summary>

This signature is generated from the current function. Arguments without a
default require input. For vectors of alternatives, the first is the default;
choose one alternative in a call.

```{r track-argument-signature, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
article_signature(extract_to_track, "extract_to_track")
```

| Decision | Choices, meaning and effective default |
|:--|:--|
| Data and grouping | `data` supplies vertices or LINESTRING features; `nc` supplies sources. `var = NULL` detects variables; `track_col = NULL` treats the input as one track, otherwise names its ID column. |
| `sampling` | `"vertices"` uses supplied observations; `"balanced"` shares subdivisions across all step limits; `"merged_steps"` retains separate distance/depth and time cuts; `"cells"` uses crossed grid-interval midpoints. Default: vertices; supplying a step with sampling omitted activates balanced. |
| Route steps | `spacing_km`, `depth_step_m`, `time_step` default to NULL: no implicit step. Set positive maximum horizontal distance, depth change and elapsed/calendar time. `time_step_seconds` is the alternative seconds-only input; do not combine it with `time_step`. |
| `time_unit` | `"seconds"`, `"minutes"`, `"hours"`, `"days"` are elapsed units (days = 24 hours); `"months"` and `"years"` are whole UTC calendar shifts, clamped at month ends. Default: `"hours"`. |
| Interpolation and Z | `interpolate_depth` / `interpolate_time`: FALSE (default) requires unchanged values between vertices; TRUE permits linear changes along the assumed segment. `z_as_depth = FALSE` rejects XYZ lines; TRUE explicitly uses LINESTRING Z as positive-down metres. |
| `method` | `"2d"` has no depth selection; `"nearest"` selects the closest valid layer to the requested depth; `"surface"` selects the physically shallowest layer; `"bottom"` selects the deepest valid layer. NULL (default) chooses 2d or nearest per variable. `"all"` returns the surface, bottom and nearest selections. |
| `statistics` | `"mean"` averages values; `"sd"` describes spread; `"se"` reports the standard error; `"min"` / `"max"` return the lowest / highest value. Default: `"mean"`; choose one or several, or NULL to omit summary statistics. |
| `weighting` | `"distance"` weights represented route length (default); `"duration"` weights elapsed time; `"equal"` gives each supported sample equal weight. Distance and duration are separate alternatives. |
| Coverage | `min_valid_fraction = 0.8` requires 80% valid requested track support; choose a fraction from 0 to 1. Invalid connections still contribute unavailable support. |
| `time_resolution` | `"auto"` follows observation precision; `"datetime"` preserves instants; `"daily"`, `"monthly"`, `"yearly"` compare UTC calendar labels. `"custom"` keeps full timestamps and uses a positive difftime `custom_time_interval` through `...` as a warning threshold, not a rejection limit. Default: `"auto"`. These modes do not aggregate environmental values. |
| Columns | `lon_col`, `lat_col`, `depth_col`, `date_col` name observation columns (defaults lon, lat, depth, date). `output_col = NULL` uses automatic names; supply names to choose them. |
| `distance_model` | `"WGS84"` (default) uses ellipsoidal geodesics; `"sphere"` uses spherical distances. |
| Marine mask | `land_mask = NULL` skips connectivity checks; supply CRS-defined polygons or a single-layer raster. Polygon `mask_type = "land"` (default) marks land, `"marine"` marks sea; `mask_domain` defines known coverage. Raster `marine_values` lists numeric sea codes; NA / outside coverage are unknown. |
| Mask action and precision | `land_policy = "skip"` (default) marks invalid connections while retaining observations; `"error"` stops. `mask_step_km = 0.5` limits polyline segment length for checking geodesic curvature; it does not improve coastline resolution. |
| Safety limits | `max_samples = 100000L` caps generated positions; `max_segment_km = NULL` and `max_gap_hours = NULL` disable connection limits until positive values are supplied. |
| Messages | `quiet = FALSE` (default) permits ordinary reports; TRUE hides them. Timezone and scientific warnings remain active. |

The arguments passed through `...` are restricted to the following point
selection options. Their defaults are also read from the current point function:

```{r track-forwarded-defaults, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
forwarded <- c(
  "file_col", "lon_dim", "lat_dim", "depth_dim", "time_dim", "time_match",
  "max_time_diff", "custom_time_interval", "spatial_match", "max_distance_km",
  "time_report", "spatial_report", "depth_report", "verbose"
)
defaults <- formals(extract_to_point)[forwarded]
print(knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Argument = forwarded,
  Default = vapply(defaults, function(x) paste(deparse(x), collapse = " "),
                   character(1)),
  Meaning = article_selection_notes(forwarded)
)))
```

`quiet = TRUE` overrides ordinary report switches. The inherited
`time_step_seconds` argument expresses an elapsed-time step in seconds and
cannot be combined with `time_step`. See
[`extract_to_track()`](../reference/extract_to_track.html) for all restrictions,
units and output columns, including sampling counts and actual provenance.

</details>
